overview.headline: How constitutional amendments are proposed and ratified

keyPoints.point: Students learn that authority to amend the Constitution is derived from Article V.
keyPoints.quote: The authority to amend the Constitution of the United States is derived from Article V of the Constitution.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that Congress may propose an amendment with a two-thirds majority vote in both chambers.
keyPoints.quote: an amendment may be proposed either by the Congress with a two-thirds majority vote in both the House of Representatives and the Senate

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the Archivist is charged with responsibility for administering the ratification process.
keyPoints.quote: the Archivist of the United States, who heads the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), is charged with responsibility

keyPoints.point: Students learn that a proposed amendment becomes part of the Constitution when ratified by three-fourths of the States.
keyPoints.quote: A proposed amendment becomes part of the Constitution as soon as it is ratified by three-fourths of the States (38 of 50 States).

keyTerms.gloss: Person charged with responsibility for administering ratification duties.
keyTerms.quote: the Archivist of the United States, who heads the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), is charged with responsibility

keyTerms.gloss: Formal process for approving a proposed amendment by the States.
keyTerms.quote: is charged with responsibility for administering the ratification process under the provisions of 1 U.S.C. 106b.

keyTerms.gloss: Form used by Congress to propose an amendment to the States.
keyTerms.quote: The Congress proposes an amendment in the form of a joint resolution.

keyTerms.gloss: Published notice that confirms an amendment has become part of the Constitution.
keyTerms.quote: This certification is published in the Federal Register and U.S. Statutes at Large and serves as official notice
